newsitem.title: UK: GOLF-U.S. STRENGTH IN DEPTH WON'T BE DECISIVE FACTOR - WALKER.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-U.S. STRENGTH IN DEPTH WON'T BE DECISIVE FACTOR - WALKER.

text.p: European captain Mickey Walker said on Wednesday she did not think American strength in depth would be a decisive factor in this week's Solheim Cup.
Walker, Europe's captain in their 1990 and 1994 defeats and their 1992 victory in the premier women's team event, conceded the United States have more strong players.
"But this week, in a match play situation, it will not matter," she said.
"In my lifetime I think America will always have more strength in depth by the sheer volume of players they have, the money in their game and the condition of their courses.
"But I believe we can field a very strong 12-player team and I think it will be a very tight contest."

The fourth biennial event begins at the St Pierre club in Wales on Friday with four foursomes and four fourballs. Foursomes and fourballs will be played again on Saturday with 12 singles matches on Sunday.

"Match play is so different from stroke play," Walker said. "At the Ryder Cup last year at Oak Hill, when you added up what everyone had won and the relative positions on the world rankings, the Americans were stronger.
"But the mentality and psychology of match play is different and Europe proved rankings don't really count for very much in a match play situation.

"It's very difficult to rank people in match play because both tours play it so little. There is very little to go on in terms of judging how somebody might perform in a match play situation and a Solheim Cup situation," she said.

Walker's opposite number, Judy Rankin, said she did not view the possibility of a U.S. defeat after their losses in the Ryder, Walker and Curtis Cups over the past 15 months as adding any pressure to her team.
"We are 13 people with a very singular desire to do this thing very well, to retain the trophy, take it home with us and make our friends and families very happy," she said.
Rankin was at pains to give the U.S. version of a controversial incident during the 1994 match.
The highly competitive Dottie Pepper -- then Dottie Mochrie -- was reported to have applauded when Europe's Laura Davies missed a putt in a fourballs match on the second afternoon.
Rankin said reports of the incident were out of proportion.
"If she were to have done that, it would be unacceptable," Rankin said.
"But what I'm told happened was that she and her partner gave each other a high five and a cheer because Laura's missed putt meant they won the hole when they thought they would probably lose it.

"In the excitement of winning the hole, Dottie may have cheered when Laura missed the putt. But the intention was for her and her partner (Brandie Burton) to congratulate each other for dodging a bullet."
Of Pepper's generally boisterous manner, Rankin said: "I put it down to Dottie having the temperament of a redhead. But she is back to blonde now and she is very charming."
